entry.title: Dacia Sandero EV – Reimagining Britain's Favourite Budget Car
entry.summary: The electric car market is gradually moving beyond premium models and expensive technology, but genuinely affordable family-sized EVs remain difficult to find. For manufacturers, the challenge is finding ways to reduce costs without sacrificing the practicality and usability buyers expect. Could Dacia be better placed than most to solve that problem? With…
entry.content:
When Dacia arrived in Britain, it was the Sandero that led the charge, offering motorists something increasingly difficult to find: straightforward, attainable new-car ownership without unnecessary complications.

More than a decade later, the Romanian brand has grown into a six-model line-up, stretching from the compact Spring and Sandero to the more adventurous Sandero Stepway, Duster, Jogger and flagship Bigster, with the forthcoming Striker set to broaden its appeal further.

Dacia has built a loyal following by concentrating on everyday usability, value and honest motoring, rather than chasing premium aspirations. Now, as the industry moves towards electrification, we imagine how the Sandero could evolve into an accessible electric supermini.

Our vision retains the familiar no-nonsense character, but introduces a sharper, more contemporary design that could help bring affordable electric motoring to an even wider audience.


When the second-generation Sandero arrived in Britain in 2013, its headline price was just £5,995 in basic specification. That was a remarkable proposition, but the economics of building small, affordable cars have become considerably more challenging.

Inflation is only part of the story: increasingly demanding safety requirements, emissions legislation and the technology expected by modern buyers have all added costs, with smaller cars having far less room to absorb them. Today's Sandero starts at £14,765, while Dacia's Spring electric car undercuts it at £11,990.

The Spring offers another advantage for Renault Group, too. Its zero-emission registrations contribute towards manufacturer ZEV targets, with compliance mechanisms allowing credits and overperformance to be shared or traded.

In an increasingly regulated market, a small, relatively simple electric car could prove valuable both commercially and strategically.


There may be another opportunity for Dacia in Renault Group's developing electric-car architecture. The proposed European M1E category for smaller, value-led electric vehicles could eventually provide additional regulatory incentives, although its final rules and eligibility requirements remain important.

Dacia has already shown interest in the idea through its Hipster concept. For the Sandero, however, the bigger opportunity could be adapting existing Renault Group technology without inheriting all the expense of a more sophisticated electric model.

A smaller 27.5kWh LFP battery, as used in the Twingo, could create a genuinely city-focused entry-level version. The 36.5kWh LFP pack introduced in the entry-level Renault 5 in some European markets offers a more substantial alternative.

Alternatively, the reported 44kWh battery could provide considerably more versatility. With careful specification and cost control, Dacia could offer several levels of electric Sandero without losing sight of its central promise: affordable motoring.

If Dacia could deliver an electric Sandero from around £15,000-£18,000 while preserving genuine family-car space, it would occupy a largely uncontested space in the market.


We have also imagined how Dacia could recreate the spirit of the original Sandero Access for the electric age. Rather than filling the cabin with increasingly expensive screens and technology, our entry-level proposal takes a simpler approach.

Basic steel wheels, unpainted plastic mirror caps, conventional physical controls and a smartphone-based infotainment system could remove considerable hardware and cost. Owners would use their own devices for navigation, music and connectivity, rather than paying for a large touchscreen and associated electronics.

The Twingo's 80hp electric motor would also be more than adequate for a lightweight, city-focused Sandero, with a smaller battery helping keep the purchase price under control.

The objective would be to create a genuinely affordable alternative to the increasingly fashionable, technology-heavy Renault 5, bringing the original Sandero's accessible approach to a new generation of buyers.


Dacia has demonstrated that it can challenge larger manufacturers at the upper end of the affordable market, with well-considered models such as the Bigster and forthcoming Striker expanding its appeal without abandoning its value-led philosophy.

But perhaps its greatest opportunity lies at the opposite end of the scale. The Spring has opened the door to electric motoring at a lower price, although its compact dimensions inevitably limit its appeal for some buyers.

The Sandero could occupy that crucial middle ground, offering the space, practicality and everyday usability that made the original such a success, while bringing electric power within reach of a much wider audience.

It was the Sandero that helped establish Dacia's reputation in Britain. As Renault Group continues expanding its electric ambitions, perhaps it is also the Sandero that can help secure the brand's next chapter.

entry.title: LA Motor Show 2026: TNY Explores the Biggest Reveals from Day One
entry.summary: The Los Angeles Auto Show has always offered a fascinating window into the American automotive market, and the 2026 event is no exception. From traditional V8 muscle cars and enormous family SUVs to high-performance electric vehicles and entirely new hybrid powertrains, this year's displays reveal an industry moving in several different directions…
entry.content:
Ford arrives in Los Angeles with a reminder that its performance heritage remains very much alive. The Mustang Dark Horse SC, powered by a supercharged 5.2-litre V8 producing 795hp, takes the familiar American muscle-car formula to an altogether more serious level.

In open-top form, it feels particularly at home in Southern California, where sunshine, coastal roads and the culture of performance motoring make it a fitting attraction for the LA Auto Show.

Yet Ford's future is not confined to powerful V8s. We had hoped to learn more about its forthcoming affordable electric pickup, the Fathom, but that story is still developing.

Camouflaged prototypes have been spotted testing extensively, and with its anticipated 2027 arrival approaching, we may not have long to wait for a clearer picture of Ford's next big move.


Dodge's new Charger Scat Pack takes a different approach to performance, retaining a traditional combustion engine while embracing a new generation of technology. Its 3.0-litre twin-turbocharged SIXPACK straight-six produces 550hp, making it a formidable performance car, although it sits below the 670hp all-electric Daytona Scat Pack.

For many American buyers, however, the petrol-powered version could prove the more appealing proposition. Familiar refuelling, an aggressive exhaust note and the ability to enjoy long-distance driving without planning charging stops all count for something.

The bigger question is whether Dodge will eventually bring V8 power back to the Charger. Reports suggest a supercharged HEMI could return for 2028, although this remains unconfirmed. For now, the SIXPACK is carrying the torch, but the V8 story may not be over.


Chrysler has a long history of moving American families, having helped establish the minivan as a mainstream family vehicle more than four decades ago. The Pacifica remains the centrepiece of that legacy, and its latest Copperline edition gives the familiar formula a sharper, more distinctive appearance.

Copper-tinted 20-inch wheels, contrasting exterior detailing and carefully chosen interior accents bring a welcome touch of personality, while the practical qualities that have made the Pacifica so popular remain intact. However, Chrysler faces a much bigger challenge than keeping its minivan fresh.

Following the departure of the 300, it has been reduced to a single-model manufacturer, leaving the Pacifica carrying the entire brand. Stellantis has already indicated that several new Chrysler models are planned by 2030, including an Airflow-related addition and further unnamed vehicles.

These future family-focused products could prove far more important than any individual Pacifica update, giving Chrysler the broader range it desperately needs to reclaim its place in the American market.


Cadillac is enjoying something of a renaissance, and its latest electric models are helping restore the American marque's sense of occasion. The VISTIQ is a particularly striking example, with sharp bodywork, dramatic vertical lighting and an imposing front end that shares the visual confidence of the much larger Escalade IQ.

There is even a hint of the extravagant ambition Cadillac has demonstrated with its six-figure Celestiq, a car intended to challenge the world's most prestigious luxury manufacturers.

Yet the VISTIQ takes that design philosophy into more familiar territory: a premium, three-row family SUV.

With seating for up to seven, 615hp from its dual-motor electric powertrain and an American starting price around $78,400 for the 2027 model, it offers considerable presence without requiring Rolls-Royce money. Cadillac is increasingly finding its own identity in the electric era.


Lucid is one of California's most ambitious automotive newcomers, and the Gravity GT-S provides a good illustration of where the company hopes to go next.

This sleek, seven-seat electric SUV combines an unusually elegant design with serious performance, its dual-motor powertrain producing 1,070hp and delivering a claimed 0–60mph time of just 3.1 seconds. It is a striking addition to the Los Angeles Auto Show, particularly given the company's ambition to establish itself as a major American luxury manufacturer.

However, Lucid's future depends on reaching beyond expensive flagship models such as the Air and Gravity.

Recent financial backing from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund should help support its forthcoming, smaller electric models, including the Cosmos and Earth SUVs, which could eventually bring the brand to a wider audience. With European expansion also on the horizon, we hope a UK arrival will follow.


Although first unveiled in California in March 2024, the R2 feels particularly at home at the Los Angeles Auto Show. Now reaching customers, the smaller electric SUV represents an important step for Rivian as it looks beyond its more expensive R1S and R1T models.

More accessible in both size and price, the R2 retains the adventurous styling, practical interior and rugged character that have helped establish the brand. With more than 300 miles of estimated range in its launch specification, it offers the everyday usability expected of a modern family EV, alongside the freedom to venture further afield.

Rivian is increasingly positioning itself as a genuine challenger to Tesla, particularly the Model Y, but with a stronger emphasis on outdoor lifestyles and capability. The R2 could prove to be the model that takes Rivian from a premium EV specialist to a much broader American manufacturer.


From Rivian's American take on the electric family SUV, we move to Germany and Porsche's performance flagship: the Cayenne Turbo Electric. While Rivian is building its identity around accessibility and adventure, Porsche has taken the SUV concept to an altogether more extreme level.

With up to 1,140bhp available under launch control, the Cayenne delivers straight-line performance that only a handful of high-performance SUVs can rival. It can reach 62mph in just 2.5 seconds, figures that would have seemed extraordinary for a large family SUV only a few years ago.

Yet its styling is arguably just as interesting. The original Cayenne divided opinion with its bulky, sometimes awkward appearance; this all-electric version adopts a softer, more restrained design, retaining Porsche's familiar identity without quite the visual aggression of earlier models. It is a considerably more sophisticated-looking statement.


Hyundai is arguably one of the biggest players at this year's Los Angeles Auto Show, using the event to introduce its latest Elantra to North American audiences alongside a wider showcase of hybrid technology across the Hyundai Motor Group.

Already launched in South Korea as the Avante, the eighth-generation Elantra arrives with a much sharper interpretation of the compact saloon, adopting Hyundai's new 'Art of Steel' design language while growing in size to offer interior space approaching that of a larger family car.

The 2027 petrol model will be followed by a 2028 hybrid, pairing a 1.6-litre petrol engine with electric assistance and targeting up to 53mpg (US). The technology extends beyond Hyundai itself, with Kia and Genesis also introducing new hybrid options across their respective ranges.

It is a reminder that, while the group continues to invest heavily in electric vehicles, it sees considerable opportunity in improving the efficiency of familiar petrol-powered models too.


Kia's design team seems to be on a roll at the moment, and the latest Telluride is another strong example. Its upright proportions, distinctive lighting and confident stance give it plenty of road presence, while the redesigned interior moves the large family SUV further upmarket.

Although not officially offered in Britain, UK readers can think of it as a larger, more imposing relative of the Sorento, with dimensions closer to the all-electric EV9. The big news for 2027 is the arrival of the Telluride's first hybrid powertrain, pairing a 2.5-litre turbocharged petrol engine with electric motors to produce 329hp.

Kia estimates up to 35mpg (US) combined, while retaining seating for up to eight. It is a significant addition to the range, showing how Kia is bringing hybrid technology to even its largest family vehicles.


The G80 Hybrid is an important addition to the Genesis range, and one of the more interesting saloons on display in Los Angeles. Its elegant proportions, distinctive lighting and updated detailing give it plenty of presence, while the longer-wheelbase body places an even greater emphasis on rear-seat comfort.

Under the bonnet is a new 2.5-litre turbocharged hybrid powertrain, producing 347hp and 391lb-ft of torque, paired with a seven-speed automatic transmission. Genesis expects the system to improve fuel efficiency by around 30% compared with the conventional petrol G80, while delivering more than 500 miles of estimated range.

Although the conventional G80 is no longer offered new in the UK, Genesis continues to build its presence here, with its electric models forming the core of the current range.

The hybrid's arrival in America is a reminder that Hyundai Motor Group is taking different approaches to different markets, and has not abandoned the traditional large luxury saloon for customers who still want one.


If the G80 Hybrid demonstrates that Genesis still believes in the traditional luxury saloon, the GV80 Hybrid may be the more relevant proposition for European buyers.


Large premium SUVs remain hugely popular across the continent, and the GV80 has the imposing proportions and carefully judged styling to stand alongside established rivals. Making its North American debut in Los Angeles, the GV80 Hybrid shares its new 2.5-litre turbocharged hybrid powertrain with the G80 Hybrid, producing 347hp and 391lb-ft of torque.

Genesis expects a 24% improvement in fuel efficiency over the equivalent petrol model, with more than 500 miles of estimated range. The system also introduces a liquid-cooled hybrid battery, a first for Hyundai Motor Group.

Toyota's all-electric Highlander is an impressive addition to its American line-up, although it is unlikely to make the journey across the Atlantic. At almost 5.05 metres long, it is considerably larger than the electric Toyotas currently offered in Britain, with three rows of seating for up to seven and a distinctly family-focused brief.

The larger battery version targets up to 315 miles of range, while dual-motor models produce 338hp and offer all-wheel drive. There is a little history here for UK buyers: the previous Highlander Hybrid was briefly sold in Britain between 2021 and 2023, but never found the same audience as the considerably more popular RAV4 Hybrid.

Toyota eventually withdrew it, concentrating on higher-volume SUVs and leaving much of its premium SUV offering to Lexus. This new electric generation shows just how differently Toyota approaches the American market.


Acura has brought something rather special to Los Angeles with the NEXERA Vision, a dramatic two-seat sports coupé that looks every bit as striking as its name suggests.

Its low nose, muscular proportions, concealed lighting and butterfly doors make it a convincing showcase of what the brand's designers can achieve. However, this is more than simply an extravagant show car.

Developed at Acura's design studio in Los Angeles, the NEXERA introduces a new design language that will influence the next generation of production models, beginning with the RDX Hybrid, expected in 2028.

That means elements of its distinctive lighting signature and sculpted bodywork should eventually find their way onto much more familiar vehicles. The concept may never reach production in this form, but its influence is already planned, making it a meaningful glimpse into Acura's next chapter.


Not every interesting vehicle at the Los Angeles Auto Show has four wheels and an engine. Honda's Base Station is a lightweight, modular camping trailer designed to make family adventures more accessible, and it is arguably one of the more unusual ideas on display.

Developed by Honda's American design and engineering teams, it can be towed by relatively modest SUVs such as the CR-V. Its clever design allows the roof to raise, creating up to seven feet of standing room, while the interior can sleep four people.

Five large windows can be swapped for optional accessories, with a kitchen, external shower and air conditioning among the possibilities. Solar panels and an integrated battery provide off-grid power, too.

Making its first public appearance at the LA show, the Base Station demonstrates Honda's willingness to think beyond conventional vehicles and develop products around the outdoor lifestyles of its American customers.


The Nissan Rogue is effectively America's equivalent of our X-Trail, and this new 2027 model is particularly interesting because it previews the next generation of Nissan's family SUV. Making its public show debut in Los Angeles, the Rogue Hybrid introduces the latest evolution of Nissan's e-POWER technology to American buyers.

Its 1.5-litre turbocharged three-cylinder petrol engine acts solely as a generator, with electric motors driving the wheels – meaning it behaves much more like an electric car than a conventional hybrid.

The dual-motor, four-wheel-drive system produces 225hp, with a smoother, quieter and more responsive experience promised over its predecessor.

Our current X-Trail already uses e-POWER, but this latest system brings significant improvements and could offer a glimpse of the technology's future direction for Nissan's European family SUV.


The biggest takeaway from Los Angeles is just how varied the industry's future is becoming. Electrification continues to gather pace, but hybrid technology is also enjoying a resurgence, while traditional performance cars clearly retain an audience.

American manufacturers are developing vehicles around the scale and tastes of their home market, while international brands are increasingly tailoring their ranges to different regions. Not everything shown here will make it to Britain, but the decisions being made in California offer plenty of clues about what could be coming next.

entry.title: Nissan's Hidden Gems – From Everyday Runabouts to Performance Legends
entry.summary: The Nissan line-up makes for an interesting mix: from some of the cheapest everyday transport on the used market to genuine supercar performance, with a few overlooked alternatives in between. Here's a look at ten used Nissan and Infiniti models that deserve a closer look, whether you're after an economical city car,…
entry.content:
While the Nissan Micra is usually the obvious choice for anyone seeking an inexpensive small Nissan, its lesser-known sibling, the Pixo, makes an equally compelling case for bargain hunters.

Once Britain's cheapest new car, the Pixo was developed alongside the Suzuki Alto, sharing its straightforward mechanicals and economical 1.0-litre three-cylinder petrol engine. It isn't particularly exciting, spacious or luxurious, but that's hardly the point.

Simple engineering, proven Suzuki-sourced mechanicals and low running costs make it an appealing proposition. Real-world fuel economy of around 55mpg is achievable, too.

Best of all, examples with fewer than 90,000 miles can still be found for under £1,000, making the Pixo one of the cheapest routes into four-wheeled motoring.


Few small cars make quite the statement of the Nissan Cube. Its unusual, almost asymmetrical styling hides a surprisingly spacious five-seat cabin, with sliding rear seats and a light, airy interior.

Official UK models arrived with a 1.6-litre petrol engine, and examples with around 70,000 miles currently start at approximately £5,000. However, buyers have a much wider choice if they're prepared to consider Japanese imports, which commonly feature a 1.5-litre petrol engine and CVT automatic transmission.

These can be worth investigating, particularly for anyone wanting something a little different, but insurance should be checked before committing, as imported vehicles can attract different premiums. It's an unusual alternative to the conventional small family car.


Nissan was among the pioneers of affordable electric motoring, and the second-generation Leaf remains an appealing used buy. While standard models use a 40kWh battery, the more desirable e+ gets a larger 62kWh pack, delivering an official WLTP range of up to 239 miles.

It is a practical five-door family hatchback, with a 405-litre boot, decent performance and the benefit of genuinely inexpensive home charging. The technology isn't quite as modern as some newer rivals, particularly its CHAdeMO rapid-charging connection, but it remains a capable everyday electric car.

Prices for higher-capacity examples with around 60,000 miles start at approximately £9,000, making the e+ an increasingly tempting entry into longer-range EV ownership.


For buyers wanting something more substantial than the Leaf, the Ariya represents Nissan's next step in electric motoring. This stylish electric SUV offers a more upmarket cabin, generous passenger space and a comfortable driving experience, making it a convincing option.

Used examples now start at around £16,000, although we'd stretch the budget to approximately £19,000 for the larger 87kWh battery. Offering an official WLTP range of up to 329 miles in front-wheel-drive form, the long-range Ariya is particularly appealing for drivers who regularly cover longer distances.

With strong performance and an impressive standard of refinement, it feels like a considerable upgrade from the Leaf without requiring a luxury-car budget.


Not every bargain needs to be an obvious choice. The Nissan Pulsar is a largely forgotten family hatchback that never quite captured the British public's imagination, particularly when compared with the similarly sized Leaf electric car.

Yet the Pulsar offers plenty of practical appeal, with generous rear passenger space, a comfortable ride and a decent-sized boot. We'd seek out the 1.5-litre dCi diesel, which combines strong fuel economy with inexpensive road tax of just £20 a year on qualifying pre-April 2017 examples.

It isn't an exciting car, but it makes a convincing case as affordable everyday transport. With used examples starting below £2,000, the Pulsar proves that sometimes the most overlooked models offer the greatest value.


If the Leaf was Nissan's electric pioneer and the Pulsar its sensible family hatchback, the Infiniti Q30 was the premium alternative. Built at Nissan's Sunderland plant, the Q30 shares much of its engineering with the Mercedes-Benz A-Class, giving buyers an interesting combination of Japanese styling and German underpinnings.

There is plenty to like, particularly with the economical 1.5-litre diesel, which offers respectable performance and excellent potential for low running costs. Prices start at around £3,500, making it an intriguing alternative to the usual premium hatchbacks.

For buyers wanting something more spirited, the Q30 also offers a 1.6-litre turbocharged petrol, while the 2.2-litre diesel provides a stronger 168bhp and 350Nm.

This broader engine range gives it an advantage over the more budget-focused Pulsar, allowing buyers to choose between economy, performance and long-distance comfort. With its Mercedes connections and increasingly accessible used prices, the Q30 makes a compelling case as an affordable premium hatchback.


For buyers wanting something a little less predictable than the usual BMW 3 Series, the Infiniti Q50 makes a compelling alternative. Its sharp styling, rear-wheel-drive layout and high-quality, technology-filled cabin give it plenty of showroom appeal, even years after launch.

The 2.2-litre diesel is a particularly attractive entry point, producing 168bhp and a substantial 400Nm of torque, making it a punchy companion for longer journeys. Used examples can be found for under £4,000, representing considerable value for such a well-equipped car.

We'd also consider stretching the budget to around £7,000 for the 3.5-litre V6 hybrid. With 359bhp, it delivers serious performance while offering surprisingly respectable fuel economy for something with this much power. It's an increasingly rare sight on British roads, which only adds to its appeal.


For anyone who misses the days of big, naturally aspirated sports cars, the Nissan 370Z makes a very tempting proposition.

Its 3.7-litre V6 produces 323bhp, delivered to the rear wheels through either a manual or automatic gearbox. It's a proper driver's car, offering strong performance, an engaging driving experience and plenty of character without relying on turbochargers or electrification.

We're particularly drawn to the convertible, which adds open-top motoring to the package and, interestingly, appears to offer some of the best value in today's used market. Prices for 370Zs start at around £9,000. For a traditional V6 sports car, that's a lot of entertainment for the money.


If 323bhp from the 370Z isn't enough, Nissan's legendary GT-R takes things to another level. Its 3.8-litre twin-turbocharged V6 produces an impressive 478bhp in early UK models, rising to 562bhp in later versions, with power delivered through an advanced four-wheel-drive system and six-speed dual-clutch gearbox.

Capable of genuine supercar performance, the GT-R can accelerate from 0–62mph in around 3.5 seconds, yet it offers something many exotic rivals struggle to match: everyday usability.

There are four seats, a surprisingly useful 315-litre boot and enough refinement to make longer journeys perfectly possible. With early examples starting around £40,000, it's considerably more expensive than a 370Z, but offers an extraordinary amount of performance and engineering for the money.


After the excitement of the GT-R, it's time to return to reality with what could be Nissan's best all-rounder. The Qashqai has been one of Britain's biggest-selling family cars for years, and the third generation remains an appealing used buy.

We'd concentrate on the 1.3-litre mild-hybrid petrol, producing 138bhp and capable of returning over 40mpg in mixed driving. It's a sensible combination of performance and efficiency, wrapped in a practical, comfortable family SUV that still looks relatively fresh.

Prices start at around £7,500, while examples with approximately 70,000 miles can be found for under £10,000. Considering the third-generation model only arrived in 2021, that's impressive value for a modern family car.

Nissan's used-car range offers far more variety than you might expect, and there are bargains to be found at almost every budget. Whether it's a cheap Pixo, an electric Leaf, an overlooked Infiniti or the extraordinary GT-R, there's something here to suit very different needs.

The Qashqai remains the sensible all-round choice, but some of the less familiar models could prove even more rewarding. As ever, condition, service history and the right engine matter more than simply finding the cheapest example. Shop carefully, and Nissan's used-car catalogue has plenty to offer.

entry.title: DS N°3: A New Chapter for the Car That Helped Define DS
entry.summary: When the DS 3 arrived in 2010, it quickly became one of the standout small premium cars of its generation. Stylish, distinctive and offering plenty of personalisation, it gave buyers a convincing alternative to the MINI and helped establish DS as a name in its own right. Its successor took a very…
entry.content:
The DS 3 Crossback may have struggled to make the same impact as its predecessor, but there is still plenty to like about it. Its exterior styling remains distinctive, while the cabin is arguably its strongest feature, combining high-quality materials with quirky detailing and a design that stands apart from more conventional premium small SUVs.

It was also an important model for DS, becoming the first in the range to offer a fully electric version. Buyers could initially choose between petrol, diesel and electric power, before the UK range narrowed to hybrid and all-electric options.

With a current RRP starting at £33,385, the DS 3 is not especially cheap, but we have found pre-registered examples advertised for under £20,000. It still has plenty to offer; however, DS needs a truly standout model, and a return to the premium hatchback market looks to be its chosen direction.


Our interpretation of the DS N°3 builds on the F3VER concept first seen at the Paris Motor Show, translating its design cues into a smartly styled compact hatchback with a distinctly French character.

While its closely related Peugeot e-208 is expected to take a more technology-led approach, introducing steer-by-wire and a new generation of the i-Cockpit, the DS should place greater emphasis on premium materials, craftsmanship and comfort.

Sharing Stellantis' next-generation small-car architecture, the N°3 is expected to benefit from significant advances in electric performance and technology. An all-electric version is confirmed, although whether DS will also offer a hybrid powertrain remains unclear.

Either way, the challenge will be to create something that feels genuinely special, rather than simply a more expensive alternative to its Peugeot relation.


The original DS 3 was a genuine success, with approximately 445,000 examples sold in Europe, compared with around 91,000 of its SUV successor. Its appeal lay in its distinctive styling, huge choice of colour combinations, exceptionally efficient diesel engines and limited-run performance versions producing more than 200bhp.

However, the years since have seen DS become increasingly integrated with Citroën. What began as an attempt to establish a separate premium marque has evolved into a much closer operating relationship, with shared management, design leadership, platforms and components. Stellantis has now formally placed DS among its specialist brands, managed by Citroën, rather than treating it as an entirely independent operation.

This may make commercial sense, allowing DS to benefit from greater economies of scale, but it also raises questions about how distinctive the brand can become. With a new generation of models arriving, DS has an opportunity to establish a clearer identity and demonstrate that it can offer something genuinely different.


Our DS N°3 rendering offers one possible glimpse of where the brand could go next, but its wider transformation is already taking shape.

Two very different models are leading the way. The new DS N°7 replaces the DS 7, the brand's best-selling model, and looks a promising evolution. Its distinctive styling, upmarket interior and focus on comfort are complemented by a choice of efficient hybrid power or fully electric drive, with the long-range E-TENSE offering up to 460 miles on the WLTP cycle.

Meanwhile, the DS N°8 takes the brand in a more unusual direction. An all-electric flagship with a sleek SUV-coupé silhouette, it offers something rather different from the conventional premium SUV formula.

With its avant-garde design, impressive range and carefully crafted interior, the N°8 demonstrates that DS is prepared to explore new body styles rather than simply follow the established market. Together, they suggest a brand increasingly confident in its own identity.


Unveiled at the 2026 Paris Motor Show, the DS F3VER concept offered our clearest indication yet of the brand's future design direction. Although DS has not confirmed it as a direct preview of the production N°3, its compact proportions and hatchback-inspired silhouette make the connection difficult to ignore.

Measuring 4.19 metres long, it combines an unconventional, sculptural exterior with an emphasis on personalisation, including a customisable roof surround, extended two-tone paintwork and an evolving rear lighting signature.

DS also introduced its Design Intelligence philosophy, aiming to create greater visual impact through cleaner surfaces, fewer components and improved perceived quality. The concept is also intended to demonstrate how a compact car can deliver impressive electric range without sacrificing everyday practicality. It is an intriguing direction for a brand looking to rediscover its distinctive French character.



The next DS N°3 has an important role to play in the future of the brand. The original DS 3 proved that a small premium car could stand out through personality, clever personalisation and a little French flair, but its SUV successor never came close to matching that success.

With the N°7 and N°8 establishing a more distinctive direction at the larger end of the range, the opportunity now exists to bring that thinking into a smaller, more accessible package.

Stellantis provides the engineering, technology and economies of scale, but DS needs to offer more than familiar components wrapped in different styling. If the production N°3 can combine genuine individuality with quality, comfort and competitive electric range, it could become the standout model the brand has been missing. The challenge is considerable, but so is the opportunity.

entry.title: From Sodium to Solid-State: TNY Explores the Future of Electric Car Batteries
entry.summary: Battery technology is advancing rapidly, but what could the next generation of cells actually mean for electric-car drivers? From making affordable EVs cheaper and more practical to pushing premium models towards ever-greater ranges, new materials and manufacturing techniques could reshape the market. We use the Vauxhall Frontera Electric as our budget benchmark,…
entry.content:
The Volvo EX60 P12 AWD uses a high-nickel nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) lithium-ion battery, with a conventional liquid electrolyte rather than a solid-state design. Its cathode combines nickel, manganese and cobalt, while the anode is graphite-based.

The pack has a 117kWh gross capacity, of which 112kWh is usable, and operates on an 800V electrical architecture. Volvo claims up to 503 miles of WLTP range, supported by a dual-motor, 680hp powertrain.

The complete vehicle has a published running order mass of approximately 2,405kg; Volvo has not published a separately verified figure for the complete battery pack's own weight.


Replacing the conventional graphite anode with a silicon-rich alternative could make the EX60's battery both lighter and more energy-dense. Silicon can store considerably more lithium than graphite, potentially allowing the existing 112kWh usable pack to be reduced in weight. Our estimates suggest a potential saving of around 30–80kg, while retaining the P12's 503-mile WLTP range.

Alternatively, Volvo could use the same battery weight and physical space to accommodate more energy. A pack offering around 118–123kWh usable capacity could potentially push the P12 towards 530–553 miles, assuming unchanged vehicle efficiency.

We estimate the current NMC pack would cost around $15,000–17,000 to manufacture, compared with approximately $16,000–19,000 for this higher-capacity silicon-rich alternative.

However, silicon expands significantly during charging, placing stress on the anode and potentially accelerating degradation. Maintaining fast charging, safety and long-term durability remains a major engineering challenge.


Semi-solid-state batteries replace some of the conventional liquid electrolyte with a gel-like or solid electrolyte, potentially improving energy density, thermal stability and safety. Applied to the EX60, this could allow the existing 112kWh usable battery to become substantially lighter, with our estimates suggesting a potential saving of around 60–140kg.

Alternatively, Volvo could use a similar battery weight and physical footprint to accommodate around 120–125kWh of usable energy, potentially increasing the P12's WLTP range to approximately 539–562 miles.

However, this technology remains expensive to manufacture at automotive scale. We estimate a potential pack cost of $29,000–38,000, compared with $15,000–17,000 for conventional NMC.

Although the electrolyte could improve thermal stability, maintaining consistent performance, long-term durability and economical mass production remain significant challenges.


An all-solid-state battery could represent a much bigger step forward for the EX60, replacing its liquid electrolyte with a solid alternative and potentially using a lithium-metal anode. This could substantially increase energy density, allowing the existing 112kWh usable pack to become around 50–170kg lighter while retaining the P12's 503-mile WLTP range.

Alternatively, Volvo could use a similar battery weight and physical footprint to accommodate approximately 125–130kWh of usable energy, potentially taking the P12 towards 562–584 miles.

However, early-production costs could be substantial, with our estimates putting a complete pack at around $47,000–94,000.

The technology promises impressive energy density and potentially improved safety, but challenges remain around manufacturing consistency, maintaining contact between solid materials, lithium dendrite formation and long-term durability. Mass production at competitive prices remains a significant hurdle.

Optimising the existing LFP chemistry could be one of the most straightforward ways to improve the Frontera's battery without introducing an entirely new material. Advances in electrode coatings, particle sizing, cell manufacturing and battery-pack integration could increase energy density while reducing production costs. Better cell-to-pack designs could also reduce the amount of supporting structure required around the cells.

The existing 44kWh pack could potentially become around 10–20kg lighter, with manufacturing improvements bringing its estimated cost down from around $3,300–3,800 to $2,900–3,400. With capacity unchanged, the Frontera would retain its 186-mile WLTP range, although a small efficiency improvement could take this towards 190 miles. 

Alternatively, using the weight and packaging savings to accommodate a larger battery could potentially increase capacity to around 46–48kWh, lifting range to approximately 194–203 miles.

The advantage is that LFP already benefits from an established supply chain, relatively abundant materials and good durability. However, improvements are likely to be incremental rather than revolutionary, and LFP will still have a lower energy-density ceiling than more advanced lithium-ion chemistries. 


LMFP builds on LFP by replacing some of the iron in its cathode with manganese. This increases the battery's operating voltage, allowing it to store more energy without relying on expensive nickel and cobalt. It retains many of the cost and thermal-stability advantages associated with phosphate-based batteries, while potentially delivering around 10–20% greater energy density than conventional LFP.

With greater energy density, LMFP could make a 44kWh battery around 255–295kg, compared with an estimated 285–330kg for the existing LFP pack. We estimate a pack cost of approximately $3,000–3,600. Keeping capacity unchanged would leave the Frontera close to its existing 186-mile range, but using the improved density to increase capacity to around 48–51kWh could potentially deliver 203–216 miles.

That would offer a meaningful improvement without moving to a conventional nickel-rich NMC battery. However, manganese introduces additional challenges. Slower lithium-ion movement, reduced electrical conductivity and manganese dissolution can affect charging performance and long-term durability. Manufacturers must overcome these issues before LMFP can realise its full potential at scale.  


Sodium-ion batteries take a different approach, replacing lithium with sodium, an abundant and widely available material. Our example uses a Prussian-white cathode and a hard-carbon anode, with aluminium current collectors on both sides of the cell. This reduces reliance on several critical battery materials and could eventually offer manufacturers a cheaper alternative to lithium-based chemistries. 

Sodium-ion presents a different compromise. Its estimated 44kWh pack could weigh around 295–350kg, with a potential cost of $3,000–3,700. That means it may not immediately offer a weight or price advantage over LFP.

At the same capacity, the Frontera could still achieve a broadly comparable range, although its lower energy density could make it heavier. If the same weight and packaging allowance were retained, a more realistic capacity might be around 40–44kWh, giving an estimated 170–186 miles. 

Its appeal would instead lie in material availability, supply-chain diversification and potential cold-weather performance. However, the technology needs further development and greater manufacturing scale before it can become a commercially competitive alternative

What Does the Future Hold for EV Batteries?

The next generation of battery technology could change electric cars in ways that go far beyond extending their driving range.

For affordable models such as the Vauxhall Frontera, improvements to established LFP chemistry, the arrival of LMFP and the development of sodium-ion could help reduce costs, improve efficiency and make electric motoring more accessible. At the premium end, silicon-rich anodes and solid-state technologies could allow cars such as the Volvo EX60 to carry lighter battery packs, travel further or achieve both.

However, progress will not happen overnight. Manufacturing costs, material availability, charging performance, durability and the ability to produce cells at enormous scale will determine which technologies make it into mainstream vehicles. Some advances are already moving towards production, while others remain years away from widespread adoption.

Ultimately, the most successful battery will not necessarily be the one with the highest energy density. It will be the one that delivers the best balance of price, range, weight, reliability and practicality for the driver. And as battery technology continues to evolve, that balance could make electric cars an increasingly compelling choice.

entry.title: Big Cats, Small Prices – The Used Jaguars Worth Buying in 2026
entry.summary: There's something undeniably special about owning a Jaguar. Whether it's the elegant styling, luxurious interiors or the unmistakable soundtrack of a supercharged V8, the British marque has spent decades building cars with character. But today, some of those same cars are available for remarkably little money. Years of depreciation have brought everything…
entry.content:
We begin with one of Jaguar's most appealing modern bargains, the XE. Introduced in 2015 to challenge the BMW 3 Series and Mercedes-Benz C-Class, it combined sharp handling, handsome styling and a beautifully balanced rear-wheel-drive chassis.

Our research uncovered early 2.0-litre turbocharged petrol examples producing 240hp for under £6,000. These earlier Ford-derived petrol engines are particularly interesting alternatives to the more common Ingenium diesels, some of which have developed costly timing-chain problems.

The XE isn't perfect. Rear legroom is relatively tight, infotainment can feel dated and servicing costs remain those of a premium car. Nevertheless, for the money, few saloons offer quite the same combination of driving enjoyment and understated British character.

But before the XE, Jaguar had another compact executive saloon, and it's now even cheaper.


The X-Type arrived in 2001, bringing Jaguar ownership to a much broader audience. Although its Ford Mondeo connections attracted criticism, the X-Type offered attractive styling, comfortable interiors and a genuinely distinctive alternative to its German competitors.

Today, usable saloons can be found around £1,000, while our attention was drawn to the estate, with tidy examples available for under £2,000. Introduced in 2004, it combined Jaguar's traditional character with everyday practicality, making it particularly appealing as an inexpensive family car.

Petrol V6 models offer smooth performance, while diesels can be economical on longer journeys. However, rust around the sills, tired suspension and neglected maintenance deserve careful attention.


The XF Sportbrake takes the estate formula considerably further. Arriving in 2012, it combined the handsome styling of Jaguar's XF saloon with a spacious luggage compartment, comfortable seating and the sort of motorway refinement expected from a premium executive car.

Remarkably, our research uncovered examples from under £4,000, particularly those equipped with the 2.2-litre diesel engine. These offer a sensible balance of performance and economy, especially for drivers covering substantial annual mileages.

Higher specifications bring leather upholstery, attractive alloy wheels and generous equipment, making the XF feel considerably more expensive than its current asking price.

Buyers should check servicing, cambelt history, diesel particulate filter condition and electrical equipment. The larger V6 diesels offer stronger performance but can bring greater repair risks.

However, even the XF isn't Jaguar's grandest offering. For that, we turn to the flagship XJ.


For decades, the XJ represented the very best of Jaguar, combining effortless performance, elegant interiors and limousine-like comfort. Today, depreciation has made several generations surprisingly accessible.

XJs can be found for under £4,000, while examples with V8 power have appeared around £8,000. Our research even uncovered later XJR performance models around £20,000, offering extraordinary power and luxury for the money.

The aluminium-bodied X351 generation, introduced in 2009, marked a major departure from traditional Jaguar styling. Its sweeping dashboard, digital instruments and dramatic exterior brought the flagship firmly into the modern era.

Naturally, air suspension, complex electronics and powerful engines can generate substantial repair bills, so maintenance history is essential.


Few modern Jaguars have such distinctive styling as the S-Type. Launched in 1999, its rounded headlights, prominent grille and sweeping bodywork deliberately recalled the original S-Type of the 1960s.

Although controversial when new, that retro appearance has become part of its appeal. Our research found V6 petrol examples for under £2,000, with some V8 models available around £3,000.

Inside, traditional wood veneers, leather upholstery and a comfortable driving position create an atmosphere quite different from most modern executive saloons. The 3.0-litre petrol V6 is particularly appealing, delivering smooth performance without the running costs of the larger V8.

Age-related electrical faults, cooling-system problems and automatic gearbox condition deserve attention, while the 2.7-litre diesel carries additional mechanical risks.

The S-Type represents Jaguar looking proudly backwards. Our next choice is almost the complete opposite: a car that helped push the brand into an entirely electric future.


When Jaguar introduced the I-Pace in 2018, it became one of the first established premium manufacturers to offer a dedicated, fully electric performance SUV. Its futuristic styling, advanced electric architecture and remarkable acceleration made it a genuinely pioneering British luxury car.

Originally costing around £60,000, used examples can now be found from approximately £10,000. We identified one particularly interesting example at £10,350 with battery-health information available.

Twin electric motors provide all-wheel drive and 400PS, delivering performance that remains impressive today. The spacious interior, distinctive proportions and quiet driving experience also make it an appealing alternative to conventional premium SUVs.

However, battery condition is crucial. Certain I-Pace models have been affected by serious battery safety recalls, making confirmation of completed remedies and any charging restrictions essential before purchase.

For buyers wanting Jaguar SUV practicality without relying entirely on charging infrastructure, there's another option.


The F-Pace marked Jaguar's arrival in the premium SUV market in 2016, bringing sporting handling, generous interior space and distinctive styling.

Closely related in engineering to the Range Rover Velar, the F-Pace offers much of the appeal of a larger luxury SUV while retaining Jaguar's more driver-focused character.

Our research concentrated on the 3.0-litre supercharged petrol V6, uncovering examples from £12,490. With up to 380PS in higher-output versions, these offer genuinely impressive performance.

Fuel consumption can be substantial, but the V6 avoids the particular timing-chain concerns associated with some four-cylinder Ingenium diesels. Buyers should still inspect the cooling system, transmission, suspension and service records carefully.


Jaguar's smaller E-Pace arrived in 2017, offering much of the F-Pace's styling in a more manageable package. With a comfortable cabin, attractive proportions and practical five-door layout, it makes an appealing alternative to premium compact SUVs.

Our research uncovered 2.0-litre P250 petrol versions for under £9,000, bringing 250PS performance and all-wheel-drive capability at a particularly attractive price.

However, we were especially interested in the newer P300e plug-in hybrid, with examples appearing around £15,500. Combining a 1.5-litre turbocharged petrol engine with electric rear-wheel drive, it develops 309PS and originally offered up to 34 miles of electric range.

Regular home charging could make shorter journeys particularly inexpensive, although longer petrol-powered trips will be less economical than the headline hybrid figures suggest.

For buyers who don't need SUV practicality, Jaguar's traditional sporting coupés offer an entirely different experience.


Few cars capture Jaguar's sporting character quite like the F-Type. Introduced in 2013, it combined dramatic styling, a wonderfully purposeful driving position and a range of powerful engines, creating a genuine modern successor to Jaguar's celebrated sports cars.

Our research found early F-Types from approximately £17,000, while the formidable supercharged V8 F-Type R appeared around £24,000. That's remarkable value considering the performance and presence these cars deliver.

The supercharged V6 offers a particularly appealing balance of speed, sound and relative affordability, while the V8 provides an unmistakable soundtrack and extraordinary acceleration.

Running costs shouldn't be underestimated. Tyres, brakes, cooling-system components and specialist servicing can all be expensive, making a thorough inspection particularly worthwhile.

The F-Type delivers muscle, precision and modern sporting drama. However, buyers seeking a more relaxed grand tourer, with a traditional V8 as standard, should look towards its predecessor.


We finish with one of the most tempting Jaguar bargains of all, the second-generation XK. Introduced in 2006, this elegant grand tourer combined an aluminium body, beautifully proportioned styling and a naturally aspirated 4.2-litre V8 producing approximately 300bhp.

Our research uncovered early examples from around £6,000, while later 5.0-litre V8 models appeared closer to £9,000.

Unlike the more focused F-Type, the XK prioritises long-distance comfort, with supportive leather seats, generous front-seat space and a surprisingly practical hatchback-style boot. Certain specifications also offered traditional wood veneers, including burr walnut, a popular luxury-car finish when the model launched.

The rear seats are small, and fuel consumption certainly isn't modest. Buyers should also inspect the cooling system, suspension and electrical equipment.

Nevertheless, the XK delivers an extraordinary combination of V8 performance, comfort and understated elegance for remarkably little money.


From £1,000 X-Types to V8-powered grand tourers and sophisticated electric SUVs, the used Jaguar market offers an extraordinary variety of cars at prices that would once have seemed almost impossible.

Depreciation has undoubtedly created opportunities for buyers, but choosing carefully is essential. Engine selection, maintenance history and the availability of specialist support can make the difference between an enjoyable ownership experience and an expensive mistake.

Our advice is to prioritise condition over specification, budget realistically for maintenance and consider an independent Jaguar specialist inspection before committing to a purchase.

What makes these ten cars particularly interesting is how differently they interpret the Jaguar name. Some offer traditional luxury, others impressive practicality, while the F-Type and XK deliver genuine sports-car character.

For buyers prepared to do their research, a used Jaguar can still offer something special, often for considerably less than its badge and original price might suggest.

entry.title: Reimagining Chrysler: Building the Next Generation of an American Icon
entry.summary: For over a century, Chrysler has been one of America's most recognisable automotive brands. Founded in 1925, the company built its reputation on engineering innovation, affordable luxury and distinctive American design. From the groundbreaking Airflow of the 1930s to the imposing 300 saloons and generations of family vehicles, Chrysler has helped shape…
entry.content:
Chrysler is still investing in its existing range. The 2027 Pacifica facelift introduces a striking new front end, illuminated wing badge, vertical LED lighting and updated interior details, demonstrating the brand's commitment to its current customers.

However, Stellantis' expansion plans point in a different direction. Rather than reviving the PT Cruiser or 300C, or developing a smaller Voyager, the focus is on a new family of SUVs. Historic nameplates, including Arrow and Airflow, offer a connection to Chrysler's past, while shared Stellantis platforms could make an expanded, more affordable range commercially viable.

The challenge now is creating vehicles that feel unmistakably Chrysler.


When Chrysler unveiled its Airflow concept in 2022, it offered a sleek, all-electric preview of the brand's future, alongside ambitious plans for an EV-only range. However, those plans have since changed.

After the original electric SUV programme was paused, a very different Airflow appeared briefly in a Stellantis presentation in June 2026. The newer design is more upright and practical, with sharper bodywork, distinctive vertical lighting and a full-width LED signature, all reflected in our TNY Design Studio rendering.

Expected for the 2028 model year, the new Airflow is expected to use Stellantis' flexible STLA One platform, supporting petrol, hybrid and fully electric powertrains. Early reports suggest petrol and hybrid versions could arrive first, replacing the original electric-only approach.

With pricing expected to start below $40,000, the Airflow could become an important foundation for Chrysler's expanding range.


Below the Airflow, Chrysler is planning two more affordable crossovers: the Arrow and Arrow Cross. Expected to start below $30,000, they could introduce the brand to a much broader audience, with both models anticipated around 2028.

Their foundations are already familiar in Europe. Based on the Fiat Grizzly family, both will use Stellantis' cost-effective Smart Car platform, shared with models including the Citroën C3 Aircross and Vauxhall Frontera.

The Arrow will adopt a sleeker coupé-SUV silhouette, while the Arrow Cross offers a more conventional, upright design. Petrol and mild-hybrid powertrains are expected to lead the American range, although final specifications remain unconfirmed.

Our Design Studio renderings explore how Chrysler's latest styling language could transform these affordable European foundations into something distinctly American, without the expense of developing entirely new vehicles.


The sleeker Chrysler Arrow could share its foundations with Fiat's new Grizzly Fastback, offering American buyers a more stylish alternative to the conventional SUV.

European models use Stellantis' familiar 1.2-litre turbocharged three-cylinder engine, available in petrol and mild-hybrid forms. However, American customers could be offered something different.

Stellantis has introduced a new-generation 1.6-litre turbocharged four-cylinder, manufactured in Michigan and powering the Jeep Cherokee's 210hp hybrid system. Could this engine, potentially in conventional petrol or hybrid form, find its way into Chrysler's smaller models?

Nothing has been confirmed, and adapting the engine to the Smart Car platform would require additional engineering. However, an American-built four-cylinder could offer stronger performance and greater appeal in the US market, while helping Chrysler establish a broader range of affordable vehicles.


Chrysler's future may ultimately depend on how successfully Stellantis can combine its global resources with the character and identity that made the American brand so recognisable.

The opportunity is certainly there. By sharing platforms, powertrains and components with established European models, Chrysler could introduce a broader, more competitive range without the enormous investment traditionally required to develop several new vehicles.

But affordability alone won't be enough. American buyers will expect distinctive styling, practical interiors, competitive performance and a convincing reason to choose Chrysler over increasingly capable rivals.

The Airflow, Arrow and Arrow Coupé imagined here at The New Yardstick Design Studio demonstrate how different segments could be brought together under a recognisable design language, while retaining their own personalities.

After years of contraction, Chrysler has an opportunity to become a more significant player in the American market once again. The next few years could determine whether that ambition becomes reality.

entry.title: 20 Years of Nissan Qashqai: How the Crossover Changed Britain, And What Comes Next
entry.summary: Twenty years ago, Nissan took a gamble that would help reshape Britain's car market. Rather than develop another conventional family hatchback, the Japanese manufacturer introduced something different: a practical, affordable crossover combining the everyday usability of a hatchback with the raised driving position and styling of an SUV. The Nissan Qashqai arrived…
entry.content:
When Nissan began developing a replacement for the Almera, it faced a difficult decision. Rather than compete directly with established hatchbacks such as the Ford Focus, Nissan took an entirely different direction.

The resulting Qashqai combined hatchback practicality with chunky, pseudo-off-roader styling, offering buyers the appearance and elevated seating position of an SUV without the running costs or bulk of a traditional 4x4.

Some early critics questioned the concept, but British buyers quickly embraced it. Sales exceeded Nissan's initial expectations, establishing the Qashqai as one of the manufacturer's biggest European successes. That success has endured, with more than 7.3 million Qashqai-family vehicles sold worldwide, including 4.1 million across Europe.

In 2008, Nissan expanded the range with the Qashqai+2, a stretched version offering seven seats, demonstrating just how versatile the crossover formula could become.

What initially looked like an unusual alternative to the family hatchback was rapidly becoming a blueprint for the industry.


By the time the second-generation Qashqai arrived in 2014, Nissan was enjoying a remarkable period of innovation. The GT-R had reinforced its performance credentials, the unconventional Juke had created another crossover success, and the Leaf had become the world's first mass-market, purpose-designed electric family car.

But the Qashqai remained central to Nissan's European business.

The second generation was longer, lower and more sophisticated, with sharper styling, improved interior quality and greater emphasis on technology and efficiency. The seven-seat Qashqai+2 disappeared, with Nissan directing larger families towards the X-Trail.

Crucially, the market had begun catching up. Rival manufacturers recognised the enormous potential of family crossovers, making the segment increasingly competitive.

Nissan could no longer rely on being different. It needed to demonstrate that the car which helped popularise the category could remain one of its strongest contenders.


By the arrival of the third-generation Qashqai in 2021, the crossover had become one of the most important vehicle types in Europe. Almost every major manufacturer was competing for buyers, while some brands had begun replacing traditional hatchbacks and saloons with SUVs and crossovers altogether.

Nissan responded with a more mature Qashqai, introducing fresh technology, a more spacious cabin and, subsequently, its distinctive e-POWER hybrid system.

Diesel engines disappeared from the range, leaving petrol mild-hybrid and e-POWER powertrains to meet changing customer expectations.

Competition, however, has never been fiercer. Established European, Japanese and Korean manufacturers are now joined by ambitious Chinese brands offering increasingly sophisticated and competitively priced alternatives.

The Qashqai's combination of practicality, comfort and familiar styling remains compelling, but its successor will enter a market considerably more demanding than the one Nissan helped create.


Looking at the lifespan of previous generations, a replacement for today's Qashqai might reasonably be expected around 2028 or 2029. However, recent reports suggest Nissan could instead introduce a substantial update, retaining much of the existing model's engineering.

The future of an electric Qashqai is also uncertain. Reuters reported in June 2026 that development had been halted, although Nissan has not formally ruled out an electric version. 

With the Leaf, forthcoming electric Juke and larger Ariya covering important parts of Nissan's EV range, the Qashqai could continue concentrating on petrol and hybrid technology.

Our Design Studio interpretation imagines a more modern, confident front end, incorporating Nissan's latest lighting signatures while retaining the familiar Qashqai proportions.

It's an evolutionary approach to a car whose established identity remains one of its greatest strengths.


From the rear, our proposed Qashqai continues that evolutionary approach. The familiar proportions remain, but cleaner surfaces, contemporary lighting and sharper detailing bring the design closer to Nissan's newest models.

Maintaining the Qashqai's position within Nissan's range will be particularly important. With the manufacturer investing heavily in electric vehicles, its petrol and hybrid models must remain equally competitive, offering customers a convincing alternative to going fully electric.

The next Qashqai doesn't necessarily need to reinvent the crossover. It needs to deliver the practicality, efficiency, comfort and value that made the original so successful, while introducing enough innovation to stand apart from an increasingly crowded field.

Twenty years ago, Nissan challenged the conventional family hatchback and helped change the direction of the British car market. Today, the crossover is everywhere, and the Qashqai faces more competition than ever before.

Its greatest challenge may no longer be convincing buyers to choose a crossover, but convincing them that the Qashqai is still the one to have.

But the market is changing, and some of today's discounts are surprisingly substantial. From compact car-derived vans to full-sized commercial vehicles, both brand-new and barely used electric models are…

At just £13,250 plus VAT for a brand-new example, the Citroën ë-C3 Van makes a compelling case for businesses that rarely need a full-sized commercial vehicle.

Based on the passenger ë-C3, it replaces the rear seats with a compact load area, retaining two front seats, familiar car-like driving manners and Citroën's comfort-focused suspension.

Its 44kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery offers approximately 200 miles of official WLTP range. LFP chemistry is particularly tolerant of regular charging to 100%, making more of that capacity available for everyday journeys without routinely limiting charging to 80%.

Another useful advantage is its towing capability. With a suitable approved towbar, the ë-C3 Van is rated to pull up to 550kg, potentially extending its appeal to businesses needing a small trailer. Its modest 300kg payload remains a limitation, but at this price, the little Citroën offers an appealing combination of affordability, versatility and low running costs.

TNY MARKET WATCH
DFSK EC35 39kWh 50 Auto SWB
Original manufacturer RRP £25,444 + VAT
Nearly-new price £6,995 + VAT
NEARLY-NEW SAVING £18,449 (72.5%)

Few vehicles in this comparison illustrate the unusual electric van market quite like the DFSK EC35. We found several 2024-registered examples advertised at just £6,995 plus VAT, some showing only 99 miles. Their registration dates and remarkably low mileages suggest vehicles that have seen little commercial use, although their histories should be checked individually.

Despite its modest price, the Chinese-built EC35 offers a genuinely useful 4.8m³ load area, twin sliding side doors and a claimed payload of 1,015kg. Its 38.7kWh battery provides a quoted WLTP range of up to 166 miles in the 50mph-limited version.

That speed restriction is the major compromise: this is a van for local deliveries, estates and short, predictable routes rather than regular motorway work.

Buyers should also establish battery health, warranty coverage and servicing support before purchasing. Nevertheless, the combination of commercial carrying capacity and near-delivery mileage at this price is difficult to ignore.

TNY MARKET WATCH
Ford E-Transit Courier Trend 46kWh Auto
Manufacturer RRP £27,000 + VAT
Brand-new price £16,989 + VAT
BRAND-NEW SAVING £10,011 (37.1%)

The Ford E-Transit Courier is one of the smartest-looking small commercial vehicles on sale, combining SUV-inspired styling with the practicality businesses expect from a Transit. Its compact footprint makes it easy to manoeuvre and park, yet the squared-off load area offers approximately 2.9m³ of space for tools, parcels or local deliveries.

For 2026, Ford increased usable battery capacity from 43kWh to 46kWh, lifting the official range to around 201 miles, depending on specification. Rapid charging from 10–80% can take approximately 26 minutes using a suitable DC charger, making it more flexible for businesses working beyond a fixed local route.

With brand-new examples advertised from £16,989 plus VAT, the updated van is particularly difficult to overlook when lightly used 43kWh versions can cost around £16,000. At this price, buying new offers the longer range and the reassurance of a fresh vehicle warranty.

TNY MARKET WATCH
Ford Transit City 300S 56kWh Auto L1 H1
Manufacturer RRP £29,000 + VAT
Brand-new price £18,250 + VAT
BRAND-NEW SAVING £10,750 (37.1%)

Ford's new Transit City brings an interesting proposition to the electric van market, offering substantial carrying capacity at a price normally associated with smaller commercial vehicles.

Positioned between the E-Transit Courier and E-Transit Custom, the compact L1 model provides approximately 6m³ of load space and an impressive 1,085kg payload. Its three-seat cabin, practical sliding side door and relatively compact exterior dimensions make it particularly appealing for urban deliveries and tradespeople.

A 56kWh LFP battery provides up to 158 miles of official WLTP range, while DC charging from 10–80% takes approximately 33 minutes. Although its range is modest compared with some alternatives, the Transit City prioritises everyday working capability and affordability.

With brand-new examples advertised at £18,250 plus VAT, representing a substantial reduction against the £29,000 list price, this is a particularly attractive option for businesses. Our example is advertised for delivery in December 2026.

TNY MARKET WATCH
Kia PV5 Cargo Essential 51.5kWh Standard Range L2 H1
Manufacturer RRP £27,645 + VAT
Brand-new price £21,495 + VAT
BRAND-NEW SAVING £6,150 (22.2%)

The Kia PV5 is perhaps the most futuristic-looking van in this comparison, with its clean, upright front end, distinctive lighting and unusually spacious body. Unlike a converted passenger car, it was designed from the outset as an electric commercial vehicle.

Our brand-new Standard Range Essential offer costs £21,495 plus VAT. Its 51.5kWh battery provides up to approximately 184 miles of WLTP range, while the boxy load area offers 4.4m³ of space, accommodating two Euro pallets. A low loading step makes everyday deliveries easier.

For businesses covering longer distances, the 71.2kWh Long Range Essential is also available from just £23,995 plus VAT. Its official range reaches 258 miles, providing an additional 74 miles for £2,500 more.

With modern technology, a seven-year vehicle warranty and eight-year battery cover, the PV5 looks particularly competitive for a purpose-built electric van.

TNY MARKET WATCH
Mercedes-Benz eSprinter 314 81kWh PRO Auto RWD L3 H2
Manufacturer RRP £58,850 + VAT
Nearly-new price £26,895 + VAT
NEARLY-NEW SAVING £31,955 (54.3%)

While significant discounts on smaller electric vans are becoming increasingly common, this Mercedes-Benz eSprinter stands out for its sheer size and capability.

The L3 H2 body offers an impressive 14m³ load area, paired with an 81kWh battery and rear-wheel drive. This is a full-sized commercial vehicle, suited to businesses transporting bulky goods rather than simply making short urban deliveries.

Our nearly-new 2025 example has covered just two miles, yet is advertised at £26,895 plus VAT, representing a saving of more than £31,000 against Mercedes-Benz's basic list price.

Even more remarkably, we've found a brand-new, unregistered example advertised at £27,855 plus VAT, just £960 more.

There are compromises, including an official range of approximately 161 miles and a relatively modest payload for such a large van. Nevertheless, these prices make the eSprinter a particularly compelling proposition for businesses considering electric transport.

TNY MARKET WATCH
Peugeot E-Expert 75kWh Professional Standard Auto
Manufacturer RRP £41,210 + VAT
Nearly-new price £15,995 + VAT
NEARLY-NEW SAVING £25,215 (61.2%)

Few electric vans demonstrate the scale of today's discounts quite like the Peugeot E-Expert. A familiar choice among commercial fleets, the Expert is widely represented on Britain's used market, with numerous remarkably low-mileage electric examples currently advertised.

Our facelifted 2024 Professional example has covered just 143 miles and costs £15,995 plus VAT. Its 75kWh battery offers an official WLTP range of approximately 194–230 miles, depending on configuration, while the Standard body provides 5.3m³ of load space and a payload of around one tonne.

The facelift also introduces a redesigned front end, a more contemporary dashboard and a 10-inch infotainment touchscreen.

Buyers prepared to accept the older design have even cheaper choices. Pre-facelift 2024 examples with fewer than 200 miles start around £14,490 plus VAT, while we found another with 2,000 miles for £13,790. With such an abundance of nearly-new stock, the E-Expert is particularly difficult to overlook.

TNY MARKET WATCH
Renault Master E-Tech MM35 87kWh Advance Auto L2 H2
Manufacturer RRP £42,500 + VAT
Brand-new price £25,795 + VAT
BRAND-NEW SAVING £16,705 (39.3%)

The latest Renault Master is a particularly interesting entry, combining a genuinely modern large-van design with a substantial discount. Its distinctive front end and carefully developed aerodynamics help the 87kWh E-Tech achieve an official range of around 255 miles in this MM35 configuration.

The updated cabin is equally appealing, featuring a 10-inch touchscreen, practical storage and a more contemporary dashboard than many traditional commercial vehicles.

This L2 H2 version offers 10.8m³ of load space. Although larger versions provide considerably more room, the medium-length Master strikes a useful balance between carrying capacity and manoeuvrability. Its payload of approximately one tonne is worth considering for heavier loads.

With brand-new examples advertised at £25,795 plus VAT, the electric Master is now priced surprisingly close to some conventional diesel alternatives. For businesses needing a spacious van with respectable range and modern technology, it makes a compelling proposition.

TNY MARKET WATCH
Vauxhall Combo Electric 2300 Prime 50kWh Auto L1 H1
Original manufacturer RRP £33,300 + VAT
Nearly-new price £11,995 + VAT
NEARLY-NEW SAVING £21,305 (64.0%)

The Vauxhall Combo is one of Britain's most familiar compact commercial vehicles, and its electric counterpart is becoming increasingly affordable. Our 2025-registered Prime example has covered just 3,353 miles, yet costs only £11,995 plus VAT.

This earlier 50kWh model offers up to 175 miles of official WLTP range. It misses out on the improved efficiency and potential 220-mile range of the newer 52kWh facelift, but remains well suited to predictable local journeys and overnight charging.

Despite its compact dimensions, the Combo Electric provides approximately 3.3m³ of load space and an indicative 803kg payload, making it useful for tradespeople and delivery businesses.

For those needing more room, we also found a long-wheelbase example with fewer than 100 miles advertised at £13,995 plus VAT.

With its established design, practical cabin and familiar driving experience, the Combo Electric offers considerable value for businesses willing to accept the shorter range.

TNY MARKET WATCH
Vauxhall Movano Electric 110kWh Prime Auto L3 H2
Original manufacturer RRP £50,385 + VAT
Nearly-new price £24,495 + VAT
NEARLY-NEW SAVING £25,890 (51.4%)

The Vauxhall Movano Electric rounds off our selection with one of the largest batteries available in this comparison. Our 2025-registered example has covered just 3,399 miles, yet is advertised at £24,495 plus VAT, less than half its original basic list price.

Its substantial 110kWh battery provides an official calculated combined range of approximately 235 miles in 3.5-tonne L3 H2 specification. The spacious 13m³ load area makes it suitable for bulky deliveries, removals and businesses requiring considerably more room than a compact van can offer.

The large battery limits payload to around 710kg in the 3.5-tonne version. However, the heavier 4.25-tonne Movano offers greater carrying capacity and can now be driven on a standard category B licence, thanks to recent changes in UK regulations.

With its modernised cabin, strong electric motor and significant discount, the Movano demonstrates just how accessible large electric commercial vehicles are becoming.

– The most striking finding isn't simply that electric vans are becoming cheaper, but how much choice buyers now have. From the £6,995 DFSK to heavily discounted large vans from Mercedes-Benz, Renault and Vauxhall, there are options for very different businesses and budgets.

Yet the lowest asking price isn't necessarily the best deal. Payload, driving range, charging access and the journeys a van makes every day remain important considerations. A local delivery business may find an ideal bargain here, while operators regularly covering longer distances or carrying heavy loads will need to choose more carefully.

What has changed is the starting point. With brand-new vans receiving substantial discounts and barely used examples appearing at a fraction of their original list prices, electric commercial vehicles deserve a fresh look from British businesses, including those that previously considered the switch too expensive.
